claim: Digital signaling enhances robustness of cellular decisions in noisy environments.
source: Digital signaling enhances robustness of cellular decisions in noisy environments, but it is unclear how digital systems transmit temporal information about a stimulus.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws on established scientific understanding about digital signaling systems.

claim: Mathematical modeling predicted that integral of the stimulus (concentration × duration) controls the fraction of cells that activate NF-κB in the population.
source: Mathematical modeling predicted and microfluidic single-cell experiments confirmed that integral of the stimulus (or area, concentration × duration) controls the fraction of cells that activate NF-κB in the population.
evidence: The abstract states that mathematical modeling made this prediction, which was then experimentally confirmed.

claim: Microfluidic single-cell experiments confirmed that integral of the stimulus (concentration × duration) controls the fraction of cells that activate NF-κB in the population.
source: Mathematical modeling predicted and microfluidic single-cell experiments confirmed that integral of the stimulus (or area, concentration × duration) controls the fraction of cells that activate NF-κB in the population.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states experimental confirmation of the area rule.

claim: Stimulus temporal profile determines NF-κB dynamics in responding cells.
source: However, stimulus temporal profile determined NF-κB dynamics, cell-to-cell variability, and gene expression phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: Stimulus temporal profile determines cell-to-cell variability in NF-κB activation.
source: However, stimulus temporal profile determined NF-κB dynamics, cell-to-cell variability, and gene expression phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: Stimulus temporal profile determines gene expression phenotype.
source: However, stimulus temporal profile determined NF-κB dynamics, cell-to-cell variability, and gene expression phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: A sustained, weak stimulation leads to heterogeneous NF-κB activation.
source: A sustained, weak stimulation lead to heterogeneous activation and delayed timing that is transmitted to gene expression.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: A sustained, weak stimulation leads to delayed timing of NF-κB activation that is transmitted to gene expression.
source: A sustained, weak stimulation lead to heterogeneous activation and delayed timing that is transmitted to gene expression.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: A transient, strong stimulus with the same area as a sustained weak stimulus causes rapid and uniform NF-κB dynamics.
source: In contrast, a transient, strong stimulus with the same area caused rapid and uniform dynamics.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: Digital NF-κB signaling enables multidimensional control of cellular phenotype via input profile.
source: These results show that digital NF-κB signaling enables multidimensional control of cellular phenotype via input profile, allowing parallel and independent control of single-cell activation probability and population heterogeneity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: Digital NF-κB signaling allows parallel and independent control of single-cell activation probability and population heterogeneity.
source: These results show that digital NF-κB signaling enables multidimensional control of cellular phenotype via input profile, allowing parallel and independent control of single-cell activation probability and population heterogeneity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: The MAPK pathway converts graded progesterone input to digital output in p42 MAPK that determines oocyte maturation in Xenopus oocytes.
source: For example, observations in Xenopus oocytes showed that the MAPK pathway converted graded progesterone input to digital output in p42 MAPK that determined oocyte maturation (Petty et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Similar digital activation observations were seen for the JNK pathway.
source: Subsequently, similar observations were seen for the JNK pathway (Bagowski and Ferrell, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The scaffolding protein Ste5 mediates digital MAPK activation of mating in yeast.
source: The scaffolding protein Spe5 was found to mediate digital MAPK activation of mating in yeast (Malleshaiah et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Inflammasome signaling leads to all-or-none caspase1 activation that mediates apoptosis.
source: More recently, it was found that inflammasome signaling leads to all-or-none caspase1 activation that mediates apoptosis (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The duration of Epidermal Growth Factor (EGF) stimulation modulates ERK dynamics and controls differentiation.
source: The duration of Epidermal Growth Factor (EGF) stimulation modulates ERK dynamics and controls differentiation (Santos et al., 2007; von Kriegsheim et al., 2009; Ahmed et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Glucose sensing in plants showed that cells have gene regulatory network mechanisms to allow similar responses to a short, intense or sustained, moderate stimulus.
source: Glucose sensing in plants showed that cells have gene regulatory network mechanisms to allow similar responses to a short, intense or sustained, moderate stimulus (Fu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Lymphocytes must precisely measure both antigen affinity and frequency to decide differentiation and proliferation.
source: Lymphocytes must precisely measure both antigen affinity and frequency to decide differentiation and proliferation (Iezzi et al., 1998; Gottschalk et al., 2012; Miskov-Zivanov et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NF-κB is a critical regulator of phenotype in immunity and disease.
source: NF-κB is a critical regulator of phenotype in immunity and disease (Hayden and Ghosh, 2008) and responds digitally to Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF) stimulation (Tay et al., 2010; Turner et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: NF-κB responds digitally to Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF) stimulation.
source: NF-κB is a critical regulator of phenotype in immunity and disease (Hayden and Ghosh, 2008) and responds digitally to Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF) stimulation (Tay et al., 2010; Turner et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NF-κB activation occurs for a multitude of cell stress and inflammatory signals that converge on the IKK signaling hub.
source: NF-κB activation occurs for a multitude of cell stress and inflammatory signals that converge on the IKK (IκB Kinase) signaling hub, which induces degradation of the cytoplasmic inhibitor IκB and liberates NF-κB to enter the nucleus and regulate gene expression (Hayden and Ghosh, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: IKK induces degradation of the cytoplasmic inhibitor IκB and liberates NF-κB to enter the nucleus and regulate gene expression.
source: NF-κB activation occurs for a multitude of cell stress and inflammatory signals that converge on the IKK (IκB Kinase) signaling hub, which induces degradation of the cytoplasmic inhibitor IκB and liberates NF-κB to enter the nucleus and regulate gene expression (Hayden and Ghosh, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Multi-layered negative and positive feedback lead to complex NF-κB pathway dynamics including oscillations.
source: Multi-layered negative and positive feedback lead to complex pathway dynamics including oscillations (Hoffmann et al., 2002; Nelson et al., 2004; Tay et al., 2010; Kellogg and Tay, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Dynamic NF-κB activation is involved in input–output specificity and information transmission.
source: Although it is not fully resolved how NF-κB coordinates gene and phenotype regulation, it is known that dynamic NF-κB activation is involved in input–output specificity and information transmission (Werner et al., 2005; Ashall et al., 2009; Behar and Hoffmann, 2013; Selimkhanov et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The core IκB-NF-κB regulatory module is well-studied and appears largely consistent across multiple stimulation contexts.
source: The core IκB-NF-κB regulatory module is well-studied and appears largely consistent across multiple stimulation contexts (Hoffmann et al., 2002; Nelson et al., 2004; Tay et al., 2010; Hughey et al., 2014); however, the role of module upstream of IKK activation including receptor-ligand binding and adaptor protein assembly in input-encoding remains unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: LPS induces NF-κB activation in a digital way where cells respond in an all-or-none fashion.
source: We found that lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induces NF-κB activation in a digital way where cells respond in an all-or-none fashion, but in a distinct manner from TNF, with greater ultrasensitivity and pronounced input-dependent activation delay.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section of the abstract.

claim: LPS induces NF-κB activation in a distinct manner from TNF, with greater ultrasensitivity and pronounced input-dependent activation delay.
source: We found that lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induces NF-κB activation in a digital way where cells respond in an all-or-none fashion, but in a distinct manner from TNF, with greater ultrasensitivity and pronounced input-dependent activation delay.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section of the abstract.

claim: LPS-exposed cells activated NF-κB in an ultrasensitive, digital fashion.
source: We found that LPS-exposed cells activated NF-κB in an ultrasensitive, digital fashion.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section.

claim: The percentage of responding cells in the population scales with LPS concentration, from 5% at 0.25 ng/ml to 100% at 500 ng/ml.
source: The population consisted of cells either responding or ignoring the LPS input, with the percentage of responding cells in the population scaling with LPS concentration, from 5% at 0.25 ng/ml to 100% at 500 ng/ml (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: When ligand is flowed continuously through the chamber to replace ligand loss due to cellular internalization, NF-κB oscillations sustain for the duration of the stimulus.
source: When ligand is flowed continuously through the chamber to replace ligand loss due to cellular internalization, oscillations sustain for the duration of the stimulus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to experimental data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Under TNF stimulation, the NF-κB initial peak becomes flatter and wider with increasing response time but unchanging onset time for decreasing input dose.
source: While both LPS and TNF are digital in preserving first peak area, the TNF-induced NF-κB initial peak becomes flatter and wider with increasing response time but unchanging onset time for decreasing input dose, while LPS experiences greater dose-dependent onset delay and timing variability and maintains a consistent peak shape (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Under LPS stimulation, NF-κB experiences greater dose-dependent onset delay and timing variability and maintains a consistent peak shape.
source: While both LPS and TNF are digital in preserving first peak area, the TNF-induced NF-κB initial peak becomes flatter and wider with increasing response time but unchanging onset time for decreasing input dose, while LPS experiences greater dose-dependent onset delay and timing variability and maintains a consistent peak shape (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The dose-response curve for LPS has a Hill coefficient of 2.3.
source: The dose-response curve for LPS was steeper than that for TNF (fitted to Hill dynamics reveals Hill coefficients of 2.3 and 1.5, respectively) (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The dose-response curve for TNF has a Hill coefficient of 1.5.
source: The dose-response curve for LPS was steeper than that for TNF (fitted to Hill dynamics reveals Hill coefficients of 2.3 and 1.5, respectively) (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to experimental data shown in figures.

claim: High-dose long duration LPS input causes a rapid NF-κB response with the response peak occurring at approximately 35 min after stimulation.
source: High-dose long duration input caused a rapid response with the response peak occurring at approximately 35 min after stimulation.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section.

claim: Low-dose long duration (LL) LPS input leads to a pronounced statistically significant delay in the NF-κB response.
source: In contrast, low-dose long duration (LL) input led to a pronounced statistically significant delay in the response (Figure 2C,D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to experimental data and statistical analysis shown in figures.

claim: At lowest LPS doses, the median delay until the peak of the NF-κB response exceeds 80 min with heterogeneity in the response timing between cells.
source: At lowest doses, the median delay until the peak of the response exceeded 80 min with heterogeneity in the response timing between cells (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Gene expression of early and intermediate genes exhibits a dose-dependent delay under LPS stimulation.
source: Notably, gene expression of early and intermediate genes exhibited a dose-dependent delay (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Under LPS stimulation, the response maintains a stereotypical peak shape that shifts later in time with lower dose.
source: While decreasing TNF dose altered the response slope, LPS response maintained a stereotypical peak shape that shifts later in time with lower dose (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Delayed gene expression observed under LPS stimulation contrasts with TNF-α input that does not induce delayed induction of these genes.
source: Delayed gene expression observed under LPS stimulation contrasts with TNF-α input that does not induce delayed induction of these genes (Tay et al., 2010; Pękalski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with citations to prior work for comparison.

claim: For early genes IκBα and A20 under LPS stimulation, gene expression peak is shifted from 30 min to 1 hr after stimulation.
source: For early genes IκBα and A20, gene expression peak is shifted from 30 min to 1 hr after stimulation.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section.

claim: IκBϵ expression shifts from maximum expression at 1 hr–2 hr and from 30 min to 2 hr for TNF mRNA under LPS input.
source: IκBϵ expression shifts from maximum expression at 1 hr–2 hr and from 30 min to 2 hr for TNF mRNA under LPS input.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section.

claim: Intermediate genes Ccl2 and Icam shift expression peaks from 1 hr to 2 hr and from 1 hr to 3 hr under LPS stimulation.
source: Intermediate genes Ccl2 and Icam shift expression peaks from 1 hr to 2 hr and from 1 hr to 3 hr (Figure 2E), respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Late genes Ccl5 and Casp4 do not reflect the delayed NF-κB activation due to slower induction kinetics.
source: Late genes Ccl5 and Casp4 do not reflect the delayed NF-κB activation due to slower induction kinetics.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section.

claim: LPS activates NF-κB by TLR4 engagement via CD14, leading to TLR4 dimerization.
source: LPS activates NF-κB by TLR4 engagement via CD14, leading to TLR4 dimerization.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the model development section.

claim: TLR4 dimers recruit MyD88, IRAK2/4, and other adaptor proteins leading to clustering and higher order assembly of Myddosome and TRAF6 lattice structures, which cooperatively activates IKK.
source: TLR4 dimers recruit MyD88, IRAK2/4, and other adaptor proteins leading to clustering and higher order assembly of Myddosome and TRAF6 lattice structures, which cooperatively activates IKK (Yin et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2010; Zanoni et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: Following IKK activation, nuclear NF-κB induces expression of IκBα, which negatively regulates NF-κB and IKK.
source: Following IKK activation, nuclear NF-κB induces expression of IκBα, which negatively regulates NF-κB and IKK, respectively (Hayden and Ghosh, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation to prior work.

claim: Experimental IκBα expression kinetics were similar for LPS and TNF, despite induction delay under LPS.
source: Experimental IκBα expression kinetics were similar for LPS and TNF, despite induction delay under LPS (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Extrinsic noise including variation in receptor-level and pathway components contributes to cell-to-cell heterogeneity in cell sensitivity and response dynamics.
source: Extrinsic noise including variation in receptor-level and pathway components contributes to cell-to-cell heterogeneity in cell sensitivity and response dynamics (Snijder et al., 2009; Tay et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: The mathematical model is based on the core IKK-NF-κB regulatory module.
source: We based our mathematical model on the core IKK-NF-κB regulatory module (Tay et al., 2010), which has been extensively validated experimentally.
evidence: This is stated in the model development section with citation to prior work.

claim: To extend the NF-κB core model for LPS, species for LPS, TLR4, and TRAF6 were added.
source: To extend the NF-κB core model for LPS, we added species for LPS, TLR4, and TRAF6 (Appendix 1) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the model development section.

claim: To introduce variability in the model, fluctuation in the number of TLR4 receptor molecules between cells was allowed.
source: To introduce variability in the model, we allowed fluctuation in the number of TLR4 receptor molecules between cells.
evidence: This is stated in the model development section.

claim: TLR4 is expressed at relatively low level compared to CD14 and varies significantly between cells in the population.
source: TLR4 is expressed at relatively low level compared to CD14 and furthermore varies significantly between cells in the population (Zanoni et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation to prior work.

claim: IKK phosphorylation by TRAF6 is modeled using Hill kinetics to account for cooperative activation due to Myddosome assembly and TRAF6 lattice formation.
source: To account for cooperative activation due to Myddosome assembly and TRAF6 lattice formation, we model IKK phosphorylation by TRAF6 using Hill kinetics.
evidence: This is stated in the model development section.

claim: The model reproduced the observed LPS induced NF-κB dynamics in single cells for different LPS doses.
source: The model reproduced the observed LPS induced NF-κB dynamics in single cells for different LPS doses (Figure 3B–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), though showed more dose-dependent first peak amplitude variation than observed in experiments.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to model simulation results shown in figures.

claim: The distinct feature of the proposed LPS model is the Myddosome formation leading to cooperative activation of IKK with a cooperativity coefficient of 4.
source: The distinct feature of the proposed LPS model is the Myddosome formation leading to cooperative activation of IKK (coopertivity coefficient = 4, note this value is distinct from the slope of the active cell fraction response curve), which simultaneously assures delay in activation observed experimentally for low doses, and steeper response curve than in the case of TNF stimulation (Figure 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the model development section.

claim: Simulations show that just as LPS concentration modulates fraction of active cells so does duration.
source: We first observed that just as LPS concentration modulates fraction of active cells so does duration.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from model simulations.

claim: Nearly all cells respond for durations exceeding 1 min at 500 ng/ml LPS.
source: Nearly, all cells respond for durations exceeding 1 min at 500 ng/ml.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from model simulations.

claim: Changing sub-minute duration of a high-amplitude signal in simulation controls fraction of active cells while maintaining uniformly timed, rapid NF-κB responses.
source: Notably, in contrast to changing concentration under constant long duration, which introduces timing delay and heterogeneity (Figures 2C, 3D), changing sub-minute duration of a high-amplitude signal in simulation controlled fraction of active cells while maintaining uniformly timed, rapid NF-κB responses (Figure 4B,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from model simulations with reference to figures.

claim: Precisely controlled stimulus duration regulates the activation of cells in the population in a strongly all-or-none manner, with 1- to 40-s duration LPS exposure (500 ng/ml) activating ∼3–88% of the population.
source: In agreement with simulation predictions, we found that precisely controlled stimulus duration regulated the activation of cells in the population in a strongly all-or-none manner, with 1- to 40-s duration LPS exposure (500 ng/ml) activating ∼3–88% of the population (Figure 5B and Supplementary Videos 1, 2).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding with reference to figures and videos.

claim: Short duration (i.e., 1 s) LPS stimulation, mimicking very brief exposure to bacteria, activates a small percentage of cells in the population.
source: Short duration (i.e., 1 s) stimulation, mimicking very brief exposure to bacteria, activated a small percentage of cells in the population.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding.

claim: Under short duration, strong amplitude (SS) input, NF-κB responses are fast and uniform.
source: Moreover, under short duration, strong amplitude (SS) input, responses were fast and uniform (Figure 5B, top row) in contrast to low, long (LL) stimulation that led to delayed, variable responses (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding with reference to figures.

claim: 3–5% activation occurs for both a 1-s short pulse at 500 ng/ml LPS (SS signal) and a 0.25 ng/ml constant input signal (LL signal).
source: For example, 3–5% activation occurred for both a 1-s short pulse at 500 ng/ml LPS (SS signal) and a 0.25 ng/ml constant input signal (LL signal) (Figure 5B, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding with reference to figures.

claim: Modulating duration of the SS signal from 1 s to 40 s (activating 3.3% and 87.5% the population, respectively) changes median response timing by less than 2 min.
source: However, modulating duration of the SS signal from 1 s to 40 s (activating 3.3% and 87.5% the population, respectively) changes median response timing by less than 2 min (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding with reference to figures.

claim: Statistical analysis indicates no significant difference in response time under varied pulse durations.
source: Statistical analysis indicates no significant difference in response time under varied pulse durations (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to statistical analysis shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Modulating concentration of the LL signal from 0.25 to 500 ng/ml (activating 4.9% and 98% of the population, respectively) changes the response time more than 35 min (reduced from 80 to 43 min).
source: In contrast, modulating concentration of the LL signal from 0.25 to 500 ng/ml (activating 4.9% and 98% of the population, respectively) changes the response time more than 35 min (reduced from 80 to 43 min).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding.

claim: While the variability in the response time scales with dose under LL stimulation, timing variability remains low under duration-modulated SS stimulation.
source: Moreover, while the variability in the response time scales with dose under LL stimulation, timing variability remains low under duration-modulated SS stimulation (Figures 4D, 5C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to figures.

claim: Brief but high pathogen load leads to uniform and strong NF-κB response in the population.
source: From an immunological perspective, this experiment indicates that brief but high pathogen load leads to uniform and strong NF-κB response in the population, while chronic low-grade pathogen exposure leads to population variability and delay.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of experimental findings.

claim: Chronic low-grade pathogen exposure leads to population variability and delay in NF-κB response.
source: From an immunological perspective, this experiment indicates that brief but high pathogen load leads to uniform and strong NF-κB response in the population, while chronic low-grade pathogen exposure leads to population variability and delay.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of experimental findings.

claim: Mathematical analytical analysis suggests that percent activating cells should scale with the input area.
source: Indeed, mathematical analytical analysis suggested that percent activating cells should scale with the input area (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from mathematical analysis.

claim: When plotted as a function of stimulus area (concentration × duration), all simulation series closely coincide, indicating that stimulus area clearly determines the percentage of cells that activate in the population.
source: However, when instead plotted as a function of stimulus area (concentration × duration), all simulation series closely coincide, indicating that stimulus area clearly determines the percentage of cells that activate in the population (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from model simulations with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: There is a reciprocal relationship between dose and duration in NF-κB switch activation.
source: This analysis revealed a reciprocal relationship between dose and duration in NF-κB switch activation (high dose requires less duration to achieve activation and vice versa).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from model simulations.

claim: For concentrations that achieve less than 100% activation, increasing the duration infinitely will not further increase the active fraction.
source: Importantly, for concentrations that achieve less that 100% activation, increasing the duration infinitely will not further increase the active fraction (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from model simulations with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: When two opposing square waves have equal area, simulation reveals an equal percentage of activating cells.
source: When we compared a constant input signal to square wave input signals, with one square wave that 'starts high' and another that 'starts low', simulation revealed an equal percentage of activating cells when the two opposing square waves have equal area (i.e., the duration is a multiple of the square wave period) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from model simulations with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: The fraction of active cells for square wave inputs matches that for a constant input signal with the same area.
source: Further, the fraction of active cells matched that for a constant input signal with the same area (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from model simulations with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: The Area Rule holds for the TNF network.
source: Performing identical simulations using a model of TNF-induced NF-κB activation (Tay et al., 2010), we found that the Area Rule held also for the TNF network (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from model simulations with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: In both the LPS amplitude-modulated and duration-modulated microfluidic experiments, stimulus area is an accurate predictor of fraction of active cells in the population.
source: We found that in both the LPS amplitude-modulated and duration-modulated microfluidic experiments, stimulus area is an accurate predictor of fraction of active cells in the population (Figure 7A), as predicted by the model simulations.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: A pulse of LPS 50 ng/ml for 100-s duration generates approximately the same responding cell percentage (51%) as a 10-s pulse at 500 ng/ml.
source: A pulse of either LPS 50 ng/ml for 100-s duration or 100 ng/ml for 50-s duration generated approximately the same responding cell percentage as a, 51% and 54% for the two inputs, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding.

claim: A pulse of LPS 100 ng/ml for 50-s duration generates approximately the same responding cell percentage (54%) as a 10-s pulse at 500 ng/ml.
source: A pulse of either LPS 50 ng/ml for 100-s duration or 100 ng/ml for 50-s duration generated approximately the same responding cell percentage as a, 51% and 54% for the two inputs, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding.

claim: Experimental findings, simulations, and mathematical analysis demonstrate how cells integrate amplitude and duration of input signals in switch-like pathway activation.
source: Together, experimental findings, simulations, and mathematical analysis demonstrate how cells integrate amplitude and duration of input signals in switch-like pathway activation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the combined results.

claim: Stimulus integral (or area) determines the effective 'probability' that a given cell activates NF-κB based on the percentage that activate in the population.
source: Stimulus integral (or area) determines the effective 'probability' that a given cell activates NF-κB (based on the percentage that activate in the population).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the results.

claim: Pathogen load (i.e., LPS dose) and duration of exposure (i.e., LPS pulse duration) are integrated by NF-κB system and together determine the population response.
source: These results indicate that the pathogen load (i.e., LPS dose) and duration of exposure (i.e., LPS pulse duration) are integrated by NF-κB system and together determine the population response.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the results.

claim: Modulating stimulus amplitude alters response dynamics by changing the amount of activation delay.
source: We showed that modulating stimulus amplitude altered response dynamics by changing the amount of activation delay.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings.

claim: Modulating stimulus duration does not affect activation delay but changes the population variability.
source: In contrast, modulating stimulus duration did not affect activation delay but changed the population variability.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings.

claim: Duration sensing allows for controlling only the population response while not affecting the single-cell response.
source: Duration sensing allows for controlling only the population response while not affecting the single-cell response, so that it is possible to achieve homogeneous dynamics and uniform phenotype in a desired proportion of cells.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of findings.

claim: Dose information is transmitted through the NF-κB digital response.
source: While dose information is transmitted through the NF-κB digital response, duration information is lost at the single-cell level.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings.

claim: Duration information is lost at the single-cell level in NF-κB digital response.
source: While dose information is transmitted through the NF-κB digital response, duration information is lost at the single-cell level.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings.

claim: Cells distinguish an SS versus LL signal profile based on NF-κB and gene expression dynamics.
source: Cells distinguish an SS versus LL signal profile based on NF-κB and gene expression dynamics.
evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claim: An intense, brief (SS) signal induces distinct dynamics than a weak, sustained (LL) signal, but the percentage of cells responding is the same in both cases.
source: We show that an intense, brief (SS) signal induces distinct dynamics than a weak, sustained (LL) signal, but the percentage of cells responding is the same in both cases (Figure 2C, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to figures.

claim: Plotting response delay as a function of stimulus area shows that SS and LL signals can be distinguished on the basis of response delay.
source: Indeed, plotting response delay as a function of stimulus area shows that SS and LL signals can be distinguished on the basis of response delay (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to Figure 7B.

claim: Cells can discern the category of the signal (whether SS or LL) for a given input area based on whether the response time falls above or below a separation line.
source: Cells can discern the category of the signal (whether SS or LL) for a given input area based on whether the response time falls above or below a separation line (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to Figure 7B.

claim: Modulating input amplitude is associated with higher timing variability than input duration modulation for controlling the fraction of active cells.
source: Modulating input amplitude associated with higher timing variability than input duration modulation for controlling the fraction of active cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Response amplitude alone does not provide sufficient information to discriminate an SS versus LL signal because response amplitude exhibits high variability between cells.
source: Because response amplitude exhibits high variability between cells, amplitude alone does not provide sufficient information to discriminate an SS versus LL signal (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Physiological cues are commonly transmitted by changing from an SS to an LL input profile.
source: Physiological cues are in fact commonly transmitted by changing from an SS to an LL input profile (Iezzi et al., 1998; Fu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Biological systems take advantage of the unique ability of digital signaling to separate control of population and single-cell dynamics.
source: Biological systems therefore appear to take advantage of the unique ability of digital signaling to separate control of population and single-cell dynamics, by modulating input area to determine the proportion of cells that activate in the population and input shape to instruct to determine phenotype outcomes in the activating subset of cells (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with reference to Figure 7.

claim: Modeling and experiments show that NF-κB activation is achieved by integrating the input: stimulus integral or area (concentration × duration) controls the percentage of cells that activate for both LPS and TNF.
source: Modeling and experiments showed that NF-κB activation is achieved by integrating the input: stimulus integral or area (concentration × duration) controlled the percentage of cells that activated for both a 'foreign' pathogen signal LPS and a 'self' immune signal TNF (population response).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings in the Discussion.

claim: Switch dynamics and gene expression phenotype vary depending on the input dose, with rapid homogeneous responses at high dose and delayed heterogeneous responses at low dose.
source: However, switch dynamics and gene expression phenotype varied depending on the input dose (single-cell response), with rapid homogeneous responses at high dose and delayed heterogeneous responses at low dose.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings in the Discussion.

claim: Dynamics of transcription factor activation determine the timing and specificity of gene expression and phenotype responses.
source: Dynamics of transcription factor activation determine the timing and specificity of gene expression and phenotype responses (Werner et al., 2005; Kobayashi et al., 2009; Purvis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Intercellular signaling systems may achieve distinct phenotype outcomes by controlling the input shape or temporal profile (whether SS or LL), while input area determines percentage of cells that respond.
source: Therefore, intercellular signaling systems may achieve distinct phenotype outcomes by controlling the input shape or temporal profile (whether SS or LL), while input area determines percentage of cells that respond (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with reference to Figure 7B.

claim: Antigen quality is encoded in the duration of receptor-antigen contact in lymphocyte signaling, with characteristic interaction times on the order of seconds.
source: Antigen quality is encoded in the duration of receptor-antigen contact, with characteristic interaction times on the order of seconds (Altan-Bonnet and Germain, 2005; Gottschalk et al., 2012; Miskov-Zivanov et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: T- and B-cell receptor binding with antigen-MHC triggers digital activation and cell fate control via NF-κB.
source: T- and B-cell receptor binding with antigen-MHC triggers digital activation and cell fate control via NF-κB (Kingeter et al., 2010; Oh and Ghosh, 2013; Gerondakis et al., 2014; Shinohara et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: A reciprocal relationship is observed between antigen quality and quantity in lymphocyte activation: Higher antigen affinity requires lower dose of antigen to trigger T-cell proliferation, and inversely, lower affinity requires higher dose.
source: A reciprocal relationship is observed between antigen quality and quantity in lymphocyte activation: Higher antigen affinity requires lower dose of antigen to trigger T-cell proliferation, and inversely, lower affinity requires higher dose (Gottschalk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: An intense, transient compared to a weak, sustained signal induces positive versus negative selection of naive thymic T cells.
source: Moreover, an intense, transient compared to a weak, sustained signal induces positive versus negative selection of naive thymic T cells (Iezzi et al., 1998) and T helper cell differentiation into alternatively CD4 or CD8 status (Adachi and Iwata, 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: An intense, transient compared to a weak, sustained signal induces T helper cell differentiation into alternatively CD4 or CD8 status.
source: Moreover, an intense, transient compared to a weak, sustained signal induces positive versus negative selection of naive thymic T cells (Iezzi et al., 1998) and T helper cell differentiation into alternatively CD4 or CD8 status (Adachi and Iwata, 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Switch-like signaling enables parallel and independent control over response probability and response dynamics.
source: We show that switch-like signaling enables parallel and independent control over response probability and response dynamics: while stimulus area (concentration × duration or antigen quantity × quality) regulates the percentage of cells that respond, the stimulus temporal profile or shape (for example, whether short-strong or low-long or antigen quality/quantity ratio) determines the response timing and gene expression phenotype in responding cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: Stimulus area (concentration × duration or antigen quantity × quality) regulates the percentage of cells that respond.
source: We show that switch-like signaling enables parallel and independent control over response probability and response dynamics: while stimulus area (concentration × duration or antigen quantity × quality) regulates the percentage of cells that respond, the stimulus temporal profile or shape (for example, whether short-strong or low-long or antigen quality/quantity ratio) determines the response timing and gene expression phenotype in responding cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: The stimulus temporal profile or shape determines the response timing and gene expression phenotype in responding cells.
source: We show that switch-like signaling enables parallel and independent control over response probability and response dynamics: while stimulus area (concentration × duration or antigen quantity × quality) regulates the percentage of cells that respond, the stimulus temporal profile or shape (for example, whether short-strong or low-long or antigen quality/quantity ratio) determines the response timing and gene expression phenotype in responding cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: Dose information is encoded in the delay timing and heterogeneity of NF-κB response.
source: Dose information is encoded in the delay timing and heterogeneity of NF-κB response.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: Modulating duration on the sub-minute timescale does not regulate NF-κB response dynamics.
source: On the other hand, modulating duration on the sub-minute timescale does not regulate response dynamics.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: Achieving control of percentage active in a population without introducing heterogeneity requires modulating duration of a high-dose input.
source: Indeed, achieving control of percentage active in a population without introducing heterogeneity requires modulating duration of a high-dose input (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Signaling dynamics mediate transfer of input dose information.
source: It was shown that signaling dynamics mediates transfer of input dose information (Selimkhanov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: While dose information is transmitted through dynamics of NF-κB activation, on short (minute) time scales duration information is lost in the single-cell response but retained in the population response (fraction of activated cells).
source: We find that while dose information is transmitted through dynamics of NF-κB activation, on short (minute) time scales duration, information is lost in the single-cell response but retained in the population response (fraction of activated cells).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: LPS exhibits greater ultrasensitivity (a steeper stimulus-response curve) than TNF.
source: Between the innate immune signals TNF and LPS, we found that LPS exhibits greater ultrasensitivity (a steeper stimulus-response curve) and more pronounced activation delay than TNF.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings in the Discussion.

claim: LPS exhibits more pronounced activation delay than TNF.
source: Between the innate immune signals TNF and LPS, we found that LPS exhibits greater ultrasensitivity (a steeper stimulus-response curve) and more pronounced activation delay than TNF.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings in the Discussion.

claim: Both greater ultrasensitivity and more pronounced activation delay for LPS compared to TNF are explained by higher cooperativity in IKK activation for LPS than for TNF.
source: Both of these features are explained by higher coopertivity in IKK activation for LPS than for TNF (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Distinct higher order adapter protein architectures may activate IKK with different effective cooperativities.
source: Distinct higher order adapter protein architectures may activate IKK with different effective coopertivities (Kazmierczak and Lipniacki, 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: The LPS-signaling response in macrophages may differ from that in 3T3 cells, including effects due to stronger auto and paracrine TNF signaling.
source: We note that the LPS-signaling response in macrophages may differ from that in 3T3 cells, including effects due to stronger auto and paracrine TNF signaling.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat in the Discussion.

claim: TNF signaling activates formation of a filamentous amyloid complex involving RIP1 and RIP3 kinases.
source: While TNF signaling activates formation of a filamentous amyloid complex involving RIP1 and RIP3 kinases, LPS signaling is mediated through helical assembly of the Myddosome complex (Lin et al., 2010), which interfaces with a TRAF6 lattice structure to activate IKK (Yin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: LPS signaling is mediated through helical assembly of the Myddosome complex, which interfaces with a TRAF6 lattice structure to activate IKK.
source: While TNF signaling activates formation of a filamentous amyloid complex involving RIP1 and RIP3 kinases, LPS signaling is mediated through helical assembly of the Myddosome complex (Lin et al., 2010), which interfaces with a TRAF6 lattice structure to activate IKK (Yin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Heterogeneity in switching threshold between cells may arise from cell-to-cell expression differences in signalosome components such as RIP1/3, MyD88, IRAK2/4, and TRAF6, leading to altered kinetics of signalosome assembly and IKK activation.
source: Heterogeneity in switching threshold between cells may arise from cell-to-cell expression differences in signalosome components such as RIP1/3, MyD88, IRAK2/4, and TRAF6, leading to altered kinetics of signalosome assembly and IKK activation.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Discussion.

claim: The switch-like character of NF-κB activation enables orthogonal control over two critical aspects of the response—probability of activation (fraction of active cells) and the heterogeneity of response—through the integral and temporal profile of the input.
source: In this study, we have shown that the switch-like character of NF-κB activation enables orthogonal control over two critical aspects of the response—probability of activation (fraction of active cells) and the heterogeneity of response—through the integral and temporal profile of the input.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: Secretion of signaling molecules often occurs in discrete or quantized way in the form of secretory bursts.
source: Secretion of signaling molecules often occurs in discrete or quantized way in the form of secretory bursts, and particularly in the case of short range paracrine signaling, cells may produce brief but intense secretion to achieve, for example, low probability but high predictability responses (non-heterogeneous dynamics).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the Discussion.

claim: In short range paracrine signaling, cells may produce brief but intense secretion to achieve low probability but high predictability responses (non-heterogeneous dynamics).
source: Secretion of signaling molecules often occurs in discrete or quantized way in the form of secretory bursts, and particularly in the case of short range paracrine signaling, cells may produce brief but intense secretion to achieve, for example, low probability but high predictability responses (non-heterogeneous dynamics).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Discussion.

claim: These results expand the repertoire of functions for digital signaling beyond increasing robustness to also facilitate multidimensional phenotype control based on temporal information in input signals.
source: Overall, these results expand the repertoire of functions for digital signaling beyond increasing robustness to also facilitate multidimensional phenotype control based on temporal information in input signals.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: p65-knockout 3T3 fibroblasts were modified using lentiviral vectors to express p65-DsRed under its endogenous promoter along with an H2B-GFP nuclear reporter.
source: We used p65-knockout 3T3 fibroblasts (courtesy Markus Covert) modified using lentiviral vectors to express p65-DsRed under its endogenous promoter along with an H2B-GFP nuclear reporter, as described previously (Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with citation to prior work.

claim: The cell line was clonally derived to express p65-DsRed at lowest detectable level to preserve near endogenous expression.
source: The cell line was clonally derived to express at p65-DsRed at lowest detectable level to preserve near endogenous expression.
